body:
Human health depends on the environment

Health involves physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of a recognised disease. Nutrition, housing, safe water, environmental cleanliness and access to healthcare affect the conditions in which people remain healthy.

The relationship between ecology and health becomes clear when environmental conditions change. Contaminated water can expose people to intestinal pathogens. Accumulated waste may attract disease-carrying organisms. Water collected in uncovered containers or other suitable breeding places can support mosquito reproduction. These risks depend on the pathogen, the environmental conditions and human exposure.

Microorganisms may be useful or harmful

Microorganisms include many bacteria, microscopic fungi, protozoa and algae. Some participate in decomposition, fermentation and nutrient cycling. For example, Lactobacillus bacteria are used in curd production, while decomposer organisms help break down organic waste.

Other microorganisms cause disease and are called pathogens. Viruses are different from cellular microorganisms because they require living host cells to reproduce. Not all bacteria, fungi or other microorganisms are harmful.

Infectious and non-infectious diseases

An infectious disease is caused by an infectious agent, such as a pathogenic bacterium, virus, protozoan or parasitic worm. The agent may spread between hosts directly or through food, water, air, a vector or another route.

Non-infectious diseases are not caused by a transmissible infectious agent. Examples include many inherited conditions, nutritional deficiencies and non-communicable conditions such as diabetes. Some diseases arise through a combination of genetic, behavioural and environmental factors.

The terms acute and chronic describe the duration or course of disease, not its cause. An acute disease generally develops or lasts over a relatively short period, while a chronic disease persists for a longer period. Both infectious and non-infectious diseases can have acute or chronic forms.

Pathogens, diseases and routes of transmission

DiseaseCausative agentMain route or vector
MalariaPlasmodium protozoan parasiteBite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
DengueDengue virusBite of an infected Aedes mosquito
CholeraVibrio cholerae bacteriumIngestion of contaminated water or food
TuberculosisMycobacterium tuberculosis bacteriumAirborne spread from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis
InfluenzaInfluenza virusExposure to infectious respiratory particles

A vector is a living carrier that transmits an infectious agent between hosts. In malaria, the mosquito is the vector and Plasmodium is the pathogen. In dengue, the mosquito is again the vector, but the pathogen is a virus. The vector and pathogen must not be confused.

How environmental conditions can create a chain of risk

Consider a community where drinking water becomes contaminated with faecal matter. A person may ingest pathogens through the water and develop an intestinal infection. The presence of the pathogen is the immediate cause, but poor sanitation, unsafe storage and inadequate water treatment may contribute to exposure.

Similarly, a mosquito-borne disease requires both a pathogen and an appropriate transmission route. Preventing mosquito breeding, reducing exposure to mosquito bites and identifying infected patients can interrupt different parts of the transmission process.

Prevention and treatment act differently

Vaccination prepares the immune system to respond more effectively to a specific infectious agent. Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria; they do not directly treat viral infections such as influenza or dengue. Appropriate treatment depends on the actual disease and clinical assessment.

Environmental prevention operates at the community level. Safe drinking water, hygienic sanitation, waste management, mosquito control and timely disease detection reduce opportunities for exposure. These measures complement, rather than replace, medical care.

Prelims focus

  • All microorganisms are not pathogens; many contribute to food production and decomposition.
  • Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Dengue is caused by a virus and commonly transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
  • Cholera is bacterial and commonly associated with contaminated water or food.
  • Acute and chronic describe disease duration, while infectious and non-infectious describe causes.
  • Trap: A vector is a carrier of a pathogen, not necessarily the pathogen itself.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections 2.1–2.3; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, sections 13.1–13.3; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, discussion of common infectious diseases; World Health Organization, Global Malaria Programme, Diagnosis and Case Management, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Ecology, Microorganisms and the Causes of Human Disease

body:
Measurement, screening and diagnosis are different

A health technology may measure a body function, screen for a possible problem or detect a specific biological marker. Diagnosis is the identification of a medical condition using the appropriate combination of symptoms, examination, measurements and investigations.

A measurement can reveal an abnormal value without identifying its cause. A screening result may suggest further investigation without establishing a definitive diagnosis. Different tests are suitable for different questions.

Common devices used for health monitoring

DeviceWhat it measuresImportant limitation
Clinical thermometerBody temperatureFever alone does not identify a specific infection.
Blood-pressure monitorArterial blood pressure, usually as systolic and diastolic valuesA single reading does not necessarily establish hypertension.
Pulse oximeterEstimated blood oxygen saturation, SpO2, and pulse rateIt does not directly diagnose the cause of low oxygen saturation.
GlucometerGlucose concentration in a small blood sampleInterpretation depends on the testing context; a single reading may not establish diabetes.
Haemoglobin measurement device or testHaemoglobin concentration in bloodA low value may indicate anaemia but does not by itself establish its cause.

Systolic blood pressure is the arterial pressure during ventricular contraction, and diastolic blood pressure is the pressure during relaxation between beats. These are commonly reported in millimetres of mercury, written as mmHg.

A fingertip pulse oximeter uses light to estimate the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen in the blood. Its reading may be affected by poor circulation, movement, skin pigmentation, temperature and nail polish. It must be interpreted alongside symptoms and clinical findings.

A pulse oximeter estimates oxygen saturation and pulse rate. It does not measure blood pressure, identify a pathogen or directly determine whether a patient needs a particular treatment.

Tests that identify an infectious agent

Infectious-disease tests may seek the organism itself or a substance associated with it. The main school-level distinctions are:

  • Microscopy: Allows trained personnel to look for visible microorganisms or parasites. In malaria diagnosis, microscopy can reveal malaria parasites in blood.
  • Antigen test: Detects a particular protein or other antigen associated with a pathogen. Malaria rapid diagnostic tests detect specified parasite antigens in blood.
  • Antibody test: Detects antibodies produced by the immune system in response to exposure. An antibody result must be interpreted according to the disease and timing; it does not always prove a current infection.
  • PCR or other nucleic-acid amplification test: Detects genetic material from the target organism. RT-PCR is used when an RNA target must first be converted into DNA for amplification.

Rapid diagnostic test describes a test designed to provide results quickly, not a single biological method. Many malaria rapid tests are antigen-based, but other rapid tests may use different technologies.

A negative test does not always exclude infection. Test performance depends on the method, the disease, the timing of sample collection and the amount of detectable target present. For some respiratory infections, molecular tests are generally more sensitive than common rapid antigen tests.

What common medical imaging technologies use

Medical imaging helps clinicians examine structures inside the body. The underlying physical principles differ:

TechnologyMain principleIonising radiation?
X-ray radiographyX-rays pass through the body and are detected to form an image.Yes
CT scanUses X-rays and computer processing to create cross-sectional images.Yes
UltrasoundUses high-frequency sound waves.No
MRIUses strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency signals.No

An imaging test reveals anatomical or functional information relevant to a clinical question. It is not interchangeable with a test that directly detects the genetic material or antigen of an infectious agent.

Monitoring over time

Repeated measurements can be more informative than one isolated result. For example, a clinician may assess a patient's temperature and oxygen saturation over time, while a public-health worker may review blood-pressure or blood-glucose measurements during follow-up. Trends must still be interpreted alongside symptoms and the reliability of the measuring device.

Prelims focus

  • A thermometer measures temperature; a blood-pressure monitor measures arterial pressure.
  • A pulse oximeter estimates SpO2 and pulse rate using light.
  • Microscopy can reveal malaria parasites; malaria rapid antigen tests detect parasite proteins.
  • PCR-based tests detect specific nucleic-acid targets.
  • X-rays and CT use ionising radiation; ultrasound and MRI do not.
  • Trap: An antigen test detects pathogen-associated material, whereas an antibody test detects the host's immune response.

[World Health Organization, Global Malaria Programme, Microscopy and How Malaria RDTs Work, consulted 3 November 2026; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Testing and Respiratory Viruses, 18 August 2025, consulted 3 November 2026; US Food and Drug Administration, Pulse Oximeters, section on use and accuracy limitations, consulted 3 November 2026; RadiologyInfo, How Much Dose Do I Get from Different Procedures?, reviewed 15 June 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Microscopy finds malaria parasites, antigen tests find pathogen proteins, molecular tests find genetic targets, and antibody tests find human antibodies.
pictures.caption: Different diagnostic methods look for different forms of evidence.

title: Diagnostic Technologies and Basic Health Measurements

body:
Why sanitation is a public-health measure

Human health depends partly on the cleanliness and safety of shared surroundings. Sanitation includes the safe collection, containment, treatment and disposal or reuse of human waste and wastewater. Hygiene includes practices such as handwashing and safe food handling that reduce exposure to harmful microorganisms.

These ideas are often grouped with safe water under WASH, meaning water, sanitation and hygiene. They are related but distinct: a household may have a toilet yet still face health risks if drinking water is contaminated or wastewater is discharged unsafely.

How faecal contamination spreads infection

Faeces from an infected person may contain disease-causing organisms. Where human waste is not safely contained, pathogens can contaminate hands, water sources, food and surfaces. Another person may become infected after swallowing the contaminated material.

Several protective measures interrupt this faecal–oral pathway:

  • Using toilets and safely managing human waste.
  • Washing hands with soap at important times, including after toilet use and before preparing or eating food.
  • Protecting drinking-water sources from contamination.
  • Using appropriate water treatment and safe storage.
  • Keeping food covered and protecting it from contamination.

Water treatment methods solve different problems

MethodMain purposeImportant limitation
SedimentationAllows heavier suspended particles to settleDoes not reliably eliminate pathogens.
FiltrationRemoves particles and, depending on the filter, some microorganismsEffectiveness depends on the filter type and its condition.
BoilingInactivates many disease-causing microorganismsDoes not remove dissolved chemical pollutants such as heavy metals.
ChlorinationDisinfects water against susceptible microorganismsDoes not remove every chemical contaminant or guarantee safety in all conditions.

Water that looks clear is not necessarily microbiologically safe. Conversely, boiling contaminated water can reduce microbial risk without removing dissolved toxic chemicals. Water quality therefore includes both microbiological safety and chemical suitability.

Safe storage matters after treatment. Water can become contaminated again if handled with dirty utensils or kept in uncovered containers.

Waste management, wastewater and vectors

Organic household waste, such as vegetable peels, can be decomposed biologically when appropriately managed. Plastic and other non-biodegradable materials require different collection and disposal arrangements. Medical sharps and infectious healthcare waste require separate handling because of the risk of injury or infection.

Wastewater must also be managed safely. At a basic level, treatment may involve removal of large solids, separation of settleable materials and biological breakdown of organic matter. Where necessary, further treatment and disinfection reduce remaining health risks.

Blocked drains and uncovered water containers may provide suitable breeding places for mosquitoes. The prevention of mosquito-borne diseases therefore includes removal or appropriate management of breeding sites, together with protection against bites. Mosquito control and drinking-water disinfection are different interventions because mosquito-borne and faecal–oral infections follow different routes.

Indian programmes connecting water and sanitation to health

Swachh Bharat Mission—Grameen

Swachh Bharat Mission—Grameen focuses on rural sanitation. The stated objectives of its Phase II include sustaining open defecation free (ODF) behaviour and improving solid and liquid waste management. Its ODF Plus approach joins continued safe toilet use with cleaner surroundings and waste-management arrangements.

ODF and ODF Plus should not be treated as identical. Sustained avoidance of open defecation is central to ODF, while ODF Plus additionally considers solid and liquid waste management and visual cleanliness under the programme's criteria.

Jal Jeevan Mission

Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide rural households with functional tap-water connections that deliver drinking water in adequate quantity, prescribed quality and on a regular basis. The prescribed quality is the Bureau of Indian Standards' IS 10500 drinking-water standard, which sets limits for microbial and chemical contaminants. The service standard is at least 55 litres per capita per day, commonly written as 55 LPCD.

The distinction between a tap connection and a functional tap connection is important. Simply installing a tap does not establish that the water supplied is safe, sufficient and regular. The programme's emphasis on reliable service delivery was reiterated in government information on Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 during 2026.

Programme classifications and implementation figures can change. The sanitation objectives and 55 LPCD service standard stated here are those described in government guidance available by 3 November 2026; they are not claims that every village or household had achieved those conditions by that date.

Prelims focus

  • WASH stands for water, sanitation and hygiene.
  • Faecal–oral transmission can occur through contaminated hands, food or drinking water.
  • Boiling reduces microbial risk but does not remove dissolved chemical contaminants.
  • Swachh Bharat Mission—Grameen Phase II includes ODF sustainability and solid and liquid waste management.
  • Jal Jeevan Mission uses a rural water-supply service standard of at least 55 LPCD.
  • Trap: A tap connection alone does not establish a safe and functional water supply.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, section on personal and community health; World Health Organization, Boil Water, technical guidance on household water safety, consulted 3 November 2026; Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Swachh Bharat Mission—Grameen, About SBM and Phase II FAQ, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Jal Shakti, Jal Jeevan Mission Operational Guidelines, section on functional household tap connections; Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 guidelines listing dated 22 May 2026; Ministry of Jal Shakti, Press Information Bureau statement on Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, 2026.]

pictures.caption: Safe sanitation and water handling break the pathway between human waste and ingestion of pathogens.

title: Safe Water, Sanitation and Prevention of Disease
